title: Yakus v. United States
lead: Wholesale meat dealers bypass a special price-regulation review process, then attempt to contest the regulation’s validity at criminal trials for exceeding its ceilings.

actors.name: Yakus and the Rottenberg petitioners
actors.role: Wholesale beef defendants convicted of willful above-ceiling sales.

actors.name: Price Administrator
actors.role: Official who issued Revised Maximum Price Regulation No. 169.

actors.name: United States
actors.role: Prosecutor defending the statute, exclusive review process, and convictions.

proceedings: The District of Massachusetts excluded regulation-invalidity proof and entered convictions on guilty verdicts.
The Supreme Court affirmed, reserving situations involving facial invalidity and diligent ongoing review.
limits: The Court did not decide whether Regulation 169 actually complied with the statute or was confiscatory. Roberts’s dissent and Rutledge’s Murphy-joined dissent dispute different aspects of the decision. This is the historical wartime scheme, not a current-law certification.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Congress gives price control a temporary wartime structure
paragraphs: The Emergency Price Control Act of 1942 sought to stabilize prices and prevent inflation, profiteering, hoarding, speculation, and disruption of production, fixed incomes, defense spending, and postwar values. Originally ending in June 1943, it was extended to June 1944. The parties did not contest Congress’s basic wartime power over commodity prices.

The Act authorized ceilings when prices rose or threatened to rise inconsistently with its purposes. Prices had to be generally fair and equitable and advance those purposes. So far as practicable, the Administrator had to consult industry, consider a specified October 1941 base period or suitable nearby representative period, and adjust for general costs, profits, and speculative fluctuations.

On December 10, 1942, the Administrator issued Revised Maximum Price Regulation No. 169 for beef and veal. Its ceilings were slightly above March 16–28, 1942 prices and approximated September 15 levels. The accompanying explanation related the base to earlier stabilization measures and explained why using October 1941 prices was impracticable.

sources.pinpoint: Facts and statutory scheme; 321 U.S. at 418–423 & nn.1–2

sections.title: The Act channels validity challenges into a special review route
sections.cue: What opportunity existed before criminal enforcement?
paragraphs: A regulated person ordinarily had sixty days from issuance to protest with specified objections and written evidence; later-arising grounds allowed later protests. The Administrator had deadlines for initial action and had to state reasons and officially noticed material when denying a protest. Within thirty days, an aggrieved protestant could complain to the Emergency Court of Appeals, composed of designated federal district or circuit judges. It could set aside unlawful or arbitrary regulations, with Supreme Court certiorari review.

The special court could not grant temporary or interlocutory injunctions. Permanent relief was delayed thirty days and, on a certiorari petition, until the Supreme Court’s final disposition. Section 204(d) made this the exclusive route for determining regulation validity, withholding that power from other federal, state, and territorial courts.

sources.pinpoint: Facts and statutory scheme; 321 U.S. at 427–430

sections.title: The defendants exceed the ceilings without invoking that process
sections.cue: What proof did the trial judge exclude?
paragraphs: Yakus and the companion Rottenberg petitioners never filed a protest or sought Emergency Court review. The protest period had expired when they were indicted in Massachusetts. At trial they offered to show that ceilings failed the statutory standards and deprived them of property because efficient wholesalers could sell only at a loss.

The District Court excluded that proof as irrelevant to the issues available at trial, rejected the constitutional and statutory objections, and entered convictions on jury verdicts. The jury found knowing violations within eight days after issuance, and the defendants did not claim lack of notice. The First Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court granted review.

The defendants challenged delegation and the exclusion of validity defenses, stressing short deadlines, written proof, lack of a judicial stay, possible punishment before a validity decision, and the choice among losing sales, stopping business, or risking penalties. They also invoked jury-trial rights and judicial power. The government defended prompt, exclusive review as necessary for uniform wartime controls.

sections.title: Stone finds legislative standards sufficient
sections.cue: Why did the delegation differ from Schechter?
paragraphs: Chief Justice Stone wrote the opinion, which Justice Roberts announced despite filing a dissent himself. The majority concluded that Congress selected the policy, the means of maximum-price regulation, and the governing conditions. An Administrator could determine complex facts, draw inferences, exercise judgment, and formulate subsidiary policy without Congress choosing the least discretionary method possible.

The question was whether the field was marked clearly enough for courts to determine compliance with legislative will. The anti-inflation purpose, fair-and-equitable limitation, base-period considerations, and explanation requirement supplied boundaries. Schechter’s broad rehabilitation purpose lacked adequate limits on permissible codes and entrusted formulation to private groups rather than a responsible official. Comparisons with upheld rate, broadcasting, competition, agricultural, and tariff schemes reinforced the result. War did not automatically remove constitutional limits.

sections.title: The majority sustains exclusive review and the lack of interim injunctions
sections.cue: Why did the defendants’ failure to use the process matter?
paragraphs: Section 204(d)’s language and history extended exclusivity to defenses in criminal proceedings, not merely independent injunction suits. Enforcement courts could assess the statute’s constitutionality, but regulation validity belonged to the special route. The Court extended Lockerty’s equity-jurisdiction reasoning to this setting.

Due process required a reasonable opportunity to be heard and offer evidence. These defendants had never tested the process or demonstrated that it could not supply one. The Court would not presume manipulated records, unsuitable evidentiary exclusions, or unreasonable delay. Rules allowed more time for evidence and oral hearings where appropriate; the Emergency Court could correct errors and authorize additional evidence. Wartime urgency made sixty days reasonable.

The ban on judicial stays likewise survived. Fragmented stays could defeat national price policy through regional disparities and delay. The statute did not compel sales, and the Administrator could modify, rescind, or suspend a regulation through available procedures. The defendants could not assume denial without applying. Injunctive relief was not absolute even for threatened irreparable harm; Congress could make the sort of public-interest judgment equity courts themselves could make. The majority analogized other urgent government measures followed by judicial review.

sources.pinpoint: Exclusive review and due process; 321 U.S. at 427–443 & nn.3–8

sections.title: A separate validity tribunal does not displace the criminal jury on violations
sections.cue: Which situations did the majority expressly reserve?
paragraphs: With an adequate independent opportunity to contest validity, Congress could criminalize willful violation and allocate validity and violation to different tribunals. Timely failure to raise even constitutional objections before a competent tribunal could forfeit them. The Emergency Court’s equitable review required no Seventh Amendment jury; the criminal jury decided whether these defendants committed willful violations.

The Court reserved a regulation unconstitutional on its face and a defendant convicted while diligently pursuing statutory review. Neither situation was presented. A ruling excluding proof that the accused had lacked an opportunity to establish invalidity remained open to constitutional review. The decision therefore did not approve excluding all constitutional defenses regardless of access to a remedy.

sources.pinpoint: Exclusive review and criminal trial; 321 U.S. at 443–448 & n.9

sections.title: Roberts and Rutledge object on different grounds
sections.cue: Why should their dissents remain separate?
paragraphs: Roberts considered the delegation insufficiently bounded. Multiple economic purposes left the Administrator free to choose competing policies, and the fair-and-equitable and base-period language imposed no real restraint. Review seemed ineffective because a protestant submitted proof before knowing the complete agency basis, while the Administrator could add studies and noticed material and enjoyed deferential review. Examples from Emergency Court decisions supported his critique. Wartime necessity could not surrender legislative functions.

Rutledge, joined by Murphy, accepted the substantive holdings, including delegation, exclusive review, and denial of interim injunctions. He objected to combining them with criminal enforcement that barred validity defenses. Power to withhold jurisdiction did not authorize courts to punish under potentially unconstitutional regulations without examining validity. A short, written civil protest process and uncertain protection against punishment were not equivalent to the criminal defense; dividing issues between tribunals was not ordinary forfeiture within successive stages of one proceeding.

Rutledge did not find the offered confiscation evidence conclusive. Neither the Constitution nor statute guaranteed every dealer a profit, and proof concerning these dealers or Boston wholesalers scarcely established inadequate margins for the trade generally. His objection remained procedural. His final note contemplated carefully safeguarded specialized proceedings equivalent to a criminal defense and a genuine opportunity to waive it, while preserving racial or religious discrimination issues in the criminal forum. He would reverse.
The Supreme Court instead affirmed the First Circuit and the convictions. It did not adjudicate the regulation’s actual conformity to the Act or its alleged confiscatory effect.

sources.pinpoint: Separate opinions; Judgment; 321 U.S. at 448–489 & Roberts nn.1–3; Rutledge nn.40–41
